newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fuji Bank wants to boost capital to improve rating.
newsitem.headline: Fuji Bank wants to boost capital to improve rating.

text.p: Fuji Bank Ltd president Yoshiro Yamamoto said his bank, one of Japan's biggest, wants to beef up its capital so it can earn a better credit rating with which to compete globally.
Yamamoto told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday that Fuji wants to aim for a rating of "AAA" -- the highest grade awarded by international credit rating agencies -- in the long-term.

"We know we cannot achieve this in the short-term, but our bank will improve step-by-step to become an AAA-rated bank." Yamamoto said. "We realise the importance of boosting our capitalisation although we haven't decided on any specific steps for that," he added.

Under rules set out by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), banks operating globally must have a capital adequacy ratio -- the ratio of a bank's capital to its risk-related assets -- of more than eight percent.
But bankers say that to compete aggressively in the international banking industry, banks need a capital adequacy ratio much higher than the required eight percent.

Yamamoto said Fuji Bank, which has assets totalling about 51 trillion yen ($463 billion), aims to raise its preliminary international capital adequacy ratio to 10 percent and stabilise it there by the business year ending March 1999.
Fuji's capital/asset ratio was 8.36 percent as of March 31.

In June, Fuji changed a corporate rule to make it possible for it to issue preferred stocks. But Yamamoto said this was only to open up more options for supporting Fuji's BIS ratio and added that the bank was not considering any new share issues at the moment.
"We haven't decided when to increase our capital. We are going to pick the right time by watching the market carefully," he said.
Meanwhile, Fuji was not considering trimming its assets to help its capital ratio, Yamamoto said.

He said Fuji was likely to sell a large number of shares it owns under cross-shareholding schemes, in which companies hold stakes in each other to strengthen ties. But at the same time, Fuji would aggressively invest in small, growing firms' shares, so its total shareholdings would stay at the same level.
The bank would also seek ways to liquidate its assets to support its capital-to-asset ratio, Yamamoto said.

Asked about the bank's earnings for the half-year ending September 30, Yamamoto said: "Our forecast figures haven't changed from the ones we have announced before. We still see a six-month parent current profit of 40 billion yen ($363 million) and six-month parent net profit of 40 billion yen ($363 million)."
Fuji believes it can achieve its parent net profit forecast of 70 billion yen ($636 million) in 1996/97 while continuing to dispose of problem loans aggressively, he said.
He said Fuji had brought its problem loans down to a manageable level. "And now, problem loans are small enough that we can cover them with our parent operating profits," he added.

Over the next several years, Fuji would put particular stress on its individual mortgage business, trust bank business and corporate business with developing companies in Japan, Yamamoto said. In the international arena, it plans to strengthen its derivatives, custody, and electrical banking business, he said. ($1=110 yen)
